summary: AE + SE meeting with Helios Health to define POC success criteria for latency/throughput SLOs. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, workload sizing (seq length, QPS, concurrency), measurement plan (synthetic vs real traffic, warm cache), and tooling for benchmarks. Agreed next steps: share benchmark spreadsheet, schedule deep-dive, and confirm production load numbers.
topics: workload sizing: seq length, QPS, concurrency
benchmark approach: synthetic vs production traffic
transcript: 00:00 - Meeting started. Quick roll call and calendar invites. Alex: ok hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Alex Rivera from Redwood. Jordan and Maya here with me. Can you hear us?
00:07 - Rachel: Yep good to go, thanks. We've got Priya and Tom as well. We're mainly here to align on SLOs for the POC, especially latency vs throughput.
00:20 - Alex (AE): Great. High level goal: we want to define measurable success criteria for a 4-week POC — specifically TTFT targets and token throughput. Jordan will lead on the measurement plan.

00:35 - Jordan (SE): Quick definitional note — in our docs we use TTFT (time-to-first-token) to capture cold-start/initial response latency and TPOT (time-per-token) to capture steady-state per-token cost/throughput. For SLAs people often want p95/p99 for both.
01:05 - Tom: For us, customer UX expects first sentence within ~200ms normally. But we can be flexible. We need to quantify across different endpoints: short chat replies vs long summarization.

01:30 - Priya: Also want to understand how warm cache and batching affect both metrics. In production caching reduces TTFT for follow-up messages; but cold starts are a problem when callers are regionally distributed.

01:50 - Jordan: Yup — measurement needs to include both cold and warm scenarios. Proposal: measure cold TTFT (no KV cache) and warm TTFT (after 1st request warms the cache). For TPOT measure steady-state with realistic batching and concurrency.

02:20 - Rachel: What's a realistic sample workload? Our median sequence length is ~60 tokens, 95th is about 420 tokens for long notes. QPS baseline is 20 QPS rising to 80 QPS at peak — concurrency maybe 40 concurrent requests at peak.

02:45 - Alex: That's helpful. We'll size tests for three buckets: short (<=64 tokens), medium (~200 tokens), long (~400 tokens). We'll run ramp tests to reach 80 QPS and soak for 30 minutes at peak to observe p99s.

03:10 - Jordan: Suggested SLOs to start: TTFT p95 <= 150ms, TTFT p99 <= 400ms for short queries (with warm cache). For long queries TTFT obviously higher — target p95 <= 300ms, p99 <= 800ms. For TPOT targets, aim for p95 <= 30ms/token and p99 <= 60ms/token for our model on NVIDIA A10/A30 style hardware equivalence. These are initial values — we'll calibrate during the POC.
03:50 - Priya: Hmm p95 150ms seems aggressive. Our UX designers want sub-200ms for common chat flows. What about network latency from our app? We need end-to-end vs service-only separation.

04:10 - Jordan: Good call — we'll measure both. Plan: report service-level metrics (Redwood inference time) and end-to-end (client -> Redwood -> client). For E2E tests we'll run from customer region to replicate network. We'll keep those separate in the benchmark sheet.
04:35 - Tom: On measurement windows — how do you suggest computing p95/p99? Rolling windows? one-minute buckets?

04:50 - Jordan: We'll capture raw latencies and compute percentiles over 1-minute and 15-minute windows. For final acceptance we'll use a 15-minute stable window during soak. Also will produce histograms and per-model breakdowns.
05:15 - Rachel: How do you handle batching and dynamic batching? We don't want increased TTFT due to batching while improving TPOT. That's a UX tradeoff.

05:30 - Alex: Exactly. For the POC we'll test multiple config axes: batching disabled (low latency), conservative batching (small batches, shorter max wait), and aggressive batching (higher throughput, longer waits). We'll show latency/throughput curves so you can pick operating point.

05:58 - Jordan: Also quantization and model variant tradeoffs. If you want lower cost we can run a quantized variant — it may change TPOT and slightly increase token-level latency. We'll include a quality check set to ensure outputs don't regress beyond your threshold.
06:20 - Priya: Good — we care about hallucination/regression checks. Please include an eval with our 50 canonical prompts.
06:35 - Alex: Noted. We'll add the canonical prompt set to the benchmark spreadsheet. Jordan will also include instructions for running it in-house or letting us run it against a hosted endpoint.

07:00 - Jordan: Measurement plan details: 1) Synthetic replay from canonical prompt set (deterministic), 2) Traffic-shaped replay (mirrors your production inter-arrival times and seq lengths), 3) Live shadow traffic if you can route it — that gives the best signal. We'll run cold-start scenarios by cycling worker pools between tests. 4) We'll collect service-side traces (TTFT, TPOT, kernel times) plus customer-side E2E latencies.
07:42 - Rachel: For the POC we can do synthetic replay and traffic-shaped replay. Shadowing will require some infra work — we may enable it later.

07:55 - Alex: Great. For POC success criteria proposal (to be explicit): a) For short/interactive flows: TTFT p95 <= 200ms and TPOT p95 <= 40ms/token during 30-minute peak soak at 80 QPS. b) For long-form flows: TTFT p95 <= 450ms and TPOT p95 <= 60ms/token. c) No >5% error rate and model output quality within your regression thresholds on canonical set. d) Cost estimate within the committed budget band.
08:35 - Priya: That reads fair. Add a p99 gate too — if p99 spikes beyond 2x p95 for more than 5 minutes it's a fail. We need stability.
08:52 - Jordan: We'll capture p99 and add an alerting rule. We'll also include percent time above threshold (SLA burn).
09:05 - Tom: On hardware: if hosted can't meet the targets we might consider Dedicated capacity or pinning to lower-latency instance types. What's typical delta between hosted and dedicated?

09:20 - Alex: Hosted usually offers good general performance, but Dedicated lets you reserve GPU pools, which reduces noisy neighbor variance and gives predictable TPOT. We'll include a performance delta estimate and cost implication in the spreadsheet.
09:38 - Rachel: For measurement artifacts we want raw latency logs, percentile calcs, and the benchmark script. Also a short runbook for reproducing tests.

09:50 - Jordan: We'll produce: benchmark spreadsheet (QPS/seq distribution/test matrix), the generator scripts (k6/postman or our harness), instructions for warm cycles, and a results dashboard snapshot. We'll link all in the follow-up email.

10:10 - Alex: Timing for the POC: proposed start next week 2027-10-18, 4-week run: week 1 infra/setup and baseline; week 2: short/medium workloads; week 3: long-form + soak; week 4: analysis, handoff, possible taper to pilot. Does that align?
10:35 - Priya: Timeline ok but need approvals internally; likely sign-off by 2027-10-15. If we can start 18th that's good.
10:50 - Rachel: We'll confirm approvals and provide sample data for traffic shaping. Also need data residency note — some tokens contain PHI; confirm KMS/HSM integration and audit logs.
11:05 - Maya (CSM): We'll include KMS integration notes and show audit log retention options. We also have a private deployment option if the hosted flow doesn't meet compliance.
11:25 - Tom: Any blockers on our side? We need a test account and temporary API key, plus the benchmark spreadsheet.
11:35 - Alex: We'll provision a short-lived API key and provide instructions. Jordan will include test harness with env vars.

11:50 - Jordan: Quick note: warm-up strategy — for KV cache we'll do a controlled warm sequence before timed tests; for batch tuning we'll measure per-request wait thresholds and queue sizes. We'll report how batching improves TPOT at cost of increased TTFT tail.
12:10 - Priya: Important: In acceptance criteria please call out whether TTFT targets are measured with or without retries and network time. Keep that explicit.
12:25 - Alex: Agreed — acceptance metrics will specify: service-side TTFT (excludes client network) and E2E TTFT (includes client network). We'll show both numbers.
12:40 - Rachel: Anything else? Oh competitors — we compared a small internal benchmark to Anthropic and OpenAI; would like Redwood to show where it sits on cost+latency.
12:55 - Jordan: We'll add a competitive slide with apples-to-apples numbers (subject to model parity assumptions).

13:05 - Alex: Ok let's recap next steps and owners. We'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and prompt set (Alex), schedule the runtime deep-dive (Jordan), send compliance docs (Maya). You (Priya) will confirm QPS and approval date. We'll tentatively start 2027-10-18.
13:30 - Priya: Sounds good. Thanks all.
13:35 - Meeting ended.
